When the Same World Bank Data Can Tell Two Stories

DSC 106 Project 2: Persuasive Visualization
Maxime Chung (mac050@ucsd.edu), Sana Gupta (svgupta@ucsd.edu), Rose Park (sep032@ucsd.edu)
Dataset: World Bank Human Development Indicators, 1960–2020. We use GDP per capita, constant 2010 US$ (NY.GDP.PCAP.KD) and life expectancy at birth, computed as the unweighted mean of the male series (SP.DYN.LE00.MA.IN) and the female series (SP.DYN.LE00.FE.IN) since the cleaned source files do not include the combined total indicator. The mean differs from the World Bank’s population weighted total by roughly 0.1 years; this does not change any conclusion drawn here.

Proposition

National income is a reliable shortcut for understanding public health outcomes.

The two sides take genuinely opposite positions on this single claim. The FOR side argues that knowing a country’s GDP per capita is enough to make confident statements about its life expectancy. The AGAINST side argues that income alone is misleading: the same data show a 20 year gap among countries the model fits worst, and many low income countries outperform their wealth on health outcomes. All four visualizations on this page draw from the same 179 country, 2019 cross section to keep the contest about visual rhetoric, not about country selection.

FOR the proposition

Two visualizations argue that income is a reliable shortcut. A log GDP regression on the 2019 cross section explains 70 percent of the variance in life expectancy. A longitudinal panel of six countries shows life expectancy and GDP rising together for six decades. If GDP is the variable you have, GDP is the variable you should use.

AGAINST the proposition

Two visualizations argue that income misses too much. The same cross section, plotted on a linear axis without a fitted curve, looks shapeless. Plotting the residuals from the FOR side’s own model surfaces a 20 year gap between the worst and best performing countries at any given income. Income predicts a great deal, but it can mislead.

FOR Visualization 1: GDP tracks 70% of the pattern

All 179 countries plotted on a logarithmic GDP axis with an OLS fit of life expectancy on log10(GDP). The fit explains 70 percent of the variance. The shaded band marks the approximate spread within which the model places about 95 percent of countries.

How to read this chart
  • Each blue dot is one country in 2019, plotted at its true GDP and life expectancy.
  • The x axis is logarithmic. GDP varies across orders of magnitude, so a log scale is the standard encoding for it.
  • The black line is the OLS fit. The legend shows the slope (+9.9 years per 10x increase in GDP) and R².
  • The shaded band is the residual spread (mean fit ± 1.96 standard deviations of the residuals), not a formal confidence interval on the regression mean.
  • Five reference countries are marked in red along the curve: Ethiopia, India, China, United States, Japan.

Design decisions

  1. +1.5
    Logarithmic x axis on GDP per capita earnest GDP per capita is exponential across countries. Log is the conventional and expressive encoding. It distributes the points evenly and reveals the underlying Preston curve. The contrast with the AGAINST side’s linear axis exposes how much rhetorical weight axis choice carries.
  2. +1
    Fitted regression line with R² disclosed in the legend earnest The fit (life expectancy = 9.9 × log10(GDP) + intercept, R² = 0.70) is shown explicitly. Plotting the fit and disclosing the goodness of fit lets the reader judge how strong the relationship is.
  3. 0
    Shaded residual spread, labeled honestly mixed The band is mean fit ± 1.96 standard deviations of the residuals; it is closer to a residual spread than to a 95 percent confidence interval on the regression mean. We label it that way in the legend and the reading guide rather than calling it a confidence band, which would have been a small but real overstatement.
  4. −1.5
    Slanted action title and subtitle deceptive "GDP Tracks 70% of the Life Expectancy Pattern" is true on the cross section but the framing nudges a reader toward reading 70 percent as the whole story. We chose "tracks" rather than "explains" or "drives" precisely to avoid causal overclaiming while still keeping the title persuasive.
  5. −0.5
    Annotate only countries that anchor the curve mixed Five countries (Ethiopia, India, China, United States, Japan) are labelled. They span the income range and sit close to the line, which trains the eye to read the chart as a curve rather than as a cloud. The AGAINST side’s outliers are not labelled here, which is asymmetric attention rather than asymmetric data.

FOR Visualization 2: across six decades, income and life expectancy climbed together

A 2019 cross section is vulnerable to the critique that maybe rich countries just happen to be old. The longitudinal answer: take six countries spanning the full income range (Ethiopia, India, China, South Korea, United States, Japan) and trace life expectancy and GDP per capita from 1960 to 2019. In every panel here, life expectancy rises alongside GDP. Gains range from +9 years (United States) to +33 years (China).

How to read this chart
  • Six panels, one per country. Same y axis (28 to 88 years) on every panel for honest comparison of life expectancy gains.
  • The blue line is life expectancy on the left axis. The gray line is GDP per capita on a logarithmic secondary axis used for context, not for direct vertical comparison.
  • Each panel carries a green badge with the total life expectancy gain from 1960 to 2019.
  • The country selection is hand picked. We do not show countries whose paths bent the wrong way; this is disclosed as a deceptive choice in the design decisions.

Design decisions

  1. +1
    Same y axis range across all six panels earnest Identical 28 to 88 year limits make magnitudes comparable across countries. Ethiopia’s gain reads as visually as dramatic as China’s. We considered per panel auto scaling and rejected it because it would have flattened Ethiopia and inflated the United States in a way that distorts the actual story.
  2. +0.5
    Logarithmic GDP on a contextual secondary axis earnest GDP per capita rose by orders of magnitude in some panels (China went from roughly $200 to $8,000). Linear GDP would crush most trajectories into an early flat line. Log is the appropriate encoding for a multiplicative variable. We label the GDP axis as contextual and not as a directly comparable vertical measure, since dual axis charts can be criticized for implying scale equivalence between two separate units.
  3. −2
    Hand picked six countries with strong upward arcs deceptive The most ethically questionable choice on the FOR side. Russia in the 1990s, Zimbabwe in the 2000s, Venezuela in the 2010s, and the Soviet collapse would each show life expectancy falling as GDP fell or stagnated. Selecting six countries whose paths all bend the same way produces a triumphal narrative the underlying data does not uniformly support.
  4. −0.5
    Cautious title that names the sample mixed The current title is "Across Six Decades, Income and Life Expectancy Climbed Together in These Six Countries." An earlier draft read "Every Path Bends Toward Longer Life," which overclaimed by implying all paths. The current title keeps the persuasive framing while staying defensible against a reader who notices the sample size.
  5. +0.5
    Annotation showing total life expectancy gain per country earnest Each panel carries an explicit "+9 yrs" or "+33 yrs" badge. The numbers are real and correctly computed. The only slant is that the comparison is across countries that all gained, which the previous decision discloses.

AGAINST Visualization 1: wealth is no cure

The same 179 countries, the same year, the same variables. The only changes from the FOR side’s first chart are the axis scaling, the absence of a fitted curve, the outlier highlights, and the title. The result reads as a shapeless cloud rather than as a curve.

How to read this chart
  • Each gray dot is one country in 2019 plotted at its true GDP per capita and life expectancy. No jitter applied.
  • Red circles: countries with substantially shorter life expectancy than the log GDP fit predicts (largest negative residuals). Equatorial Guinea, Nigeria, Lesotho, Eswatini.
  • Green squares: countries with substantially longer life expectancy than the fit predicts (largest positive residuals). Vietnam, Nicaragua, Honduras, Bangladesh. Square markers and bold text labels are used so the encoding is readable for color blind viewers.
  • The x axis is linear. Most countries collapse to a wall on the left, which is part of the persuasive effect.

Design decisions

  1. −1.5
    Linear x axis on GDP per capita deceptive GDP per capita spans almost three orders of magnitude. On a linear axis roughly 90 percent of countries collapse into a vertical wall on the left, and the Preston curve becomes invisible. We considered a square root scale as a softer alternative and rejected it because linear was more visually misleading without looking obviously broken.
  2. −1.5
    Highlight countries with the largest residuals from the log GDP fit deceptive The eight highlighted countries are the largest negative and positive residuals (computed as actual life expectancy minus the regression’s predicted value). Highlighting only outliers steers the reader toward "no relationship" rather than "strong relationship with notable exceptions." Showing every country in red or green would have been more honest but less persuasive.
  3. −1
    No fit line and no R² disclosed on this chart deceptive A regression line fitted on log GDP would yield R² = 0.70 and immediately undercut this chart’s message. Omitting the fit forces the reader to read the cloud by eye, where the linear axis already obscures the relationship. The omission is invisible to a casual reader, which is what makes it persuasive.
  4. −1.5
    Slanted action title and subtitle deceptive "Wealth Is No Cure" and "At every income level, health outcomes vary widely" prime the reader to look for variation rather than trend. We considered a neutral title ("GDP per capita and life expectancy across 179 countries, 2019") and rejected it as not persuasive enough.
  5. −0.5
    Mild y axis truncation at 50 years mixed The full life expectancy range is roughly 53 to 85 years. Starting the y axis at 50 rather than at 0 or 60 compresses the visible vertical spread slightly, which makes the cloud look more disorderly. Mild but it is the same family of choice the assignment prompt flags as a typical deceptive move.

AGAINST Visualization 2: GDP tracks 70% of life expectancy, but a 20 year gap remains

The AGAINST side accepts the FOR side’s regression line on its own terms, then plots the residuals: how far each country’s actual life expectancy lands from what its GDP per capita predicts. Even granting R² = 0.70, the unexplained 30 percent spans nearly twenty years of life. Equatorial Guinea is sixteen years below its predicted life expectancy; Vietnam is seven above. Income alone does not determine health.

How to read this chart
  • The chart uses the FOR side’s own log GDP regression to compute one residual per country.
  • Red circles: the 10 countries that live shortest relative to the GDP prediction. Equatorial Guinea is the worst (−16.0 years).
  • Green squares: the 10 countries that live longest relative to the GDP prediction. Vietnam is the best (+7.0 years).
  • The gray middle band represents the 159 other countries the model predicts within ±5 years.

Design decisions

  1. +2
    Use the opposing side’s own regression line as the baseline earnest We did not invent a new model. We took the FOR side’s log GDP fit and plotted what it leaves out. This is steel manning, not strawmanning, and it is the most earnest move in the project. A reader cannot dismiss the chart by saying "your model is wrong" because the model is the opponent’s.
  2. −1
    Show only the top 10 and bottom 10 residuals deceptive The middle 159 countries the model fits well are compressed into a single gray band. This suppresses the visual presence of the 88 percent of countries the model predicts well and elevates the 12 percent it misses. We considered showing all 179 lollipops and rejected it because the chart became unreadable and self defeating.
  3. −0.5
    Diverging palette with mark shape redundancy mixed Red and green carry pre cognitive bad and good associations that load the chart emotionally before the reader processes magnitudes. To make the encoding readable for color blind viewers we also use shape (red circles for negative residuals, green squares for positive) and explicit text labels at every lollipop end.
  4. −1.5
    Title frames the unexplained variance as a 20 year gap deceptive The 20 year figure is the actual range from worst to best residual, but the framing converts a statistical residual into a humanitarian indictment. We chose this because residuals alone are emotionally inert.
  5. +1
    Disclose R² = 0.70 in the subtitle earnest The chart explicitly tells the reader that the model the residuals come from predicts 70 percent of life expectancy variance. A more deceptive version would have buried this number. Disclosing it makes the chart fall or stand on the interpretation of the unexplained 30 percent.

Reflection

The hardest part of this project was committing to plot the same data on both sides of the cross section. Once we did, the rhetorical machinery became visible. The FOR and AGAINST first charts share every single data point. The proposition flips because of the x axis scale, a fitted curve we drew or did not draw, and a title we wrote. Working in this constraint clarified what counts as a deceptive technique versus a fair editorial choice: a log axis is not deceptive, a linear axis is not deceptive, but choosing one of them while writing a title that depends on the reader not noticing the choice is. The most satisfying chart to build was AGAINST Visualization 2, which uses the FOR side’s own regression line to plot the residuals it leaves behind, because it argues from inside the opponent’s premises rather than swapping them out.

What surprised us was how much of the persuasion lived in things we did not draw. AGAINST chart 1 is persuasive partly because there is no regression line on it. Adding the same R² = 0.70 line that appears on FOR chart 1 would single handedly undo the AGAINST argument. That asymmetric omission is, in some ways, more consequential than any positively misleading element of either chart, because nothing on the page would obviously flag it. FOR chart 2 was the inverse temptation: hand picking six countries whose trajectories all bent the right way produces a clean monotonic story that is also the project’s strongest omission. Russia in the 1990s and the post Soviet life expectancy collapse would have made an "every path" title false; we chose softer wording for that reason.

Our working definition of ethical visualization is this: a chart is ethical when the reader, given enough time, would still accept the framing (the axes, the fits, the annotations, the country selection, the title) as a defensible reading of the data. A chart is misleading when its persuasive force depends on the reader not having that time. The line we draw between persuasion and deception is the line between framing choices we would defend in public to a critical reader and framing choices that need the reader’s inattention to survive. By that test, AGAINST Visualization 2 is the most ethically defensible chart in this project (it uses the opponent’s own model and discloses R²), and FOR Visualization 2 is the most ethically questionable (it claims a six country pattern as if it were a general law). All four are persuasive, but they are not equally honest about it.

Methodology and validation

Scoring scale. Each design decision is scored from −2 fully deceptive to +2 fully earnest, in 0.5 steps. The score answers a single question: would a careful reader accept this choice as a defensible reading of the data, or would they say the chart needed their inattention to land? Scores closer to −1 rely on the reader not noticing. Scores closer to +1 survive scrutiny. Scores near 0 are roughly neutral.
  • Source files: World Bank Human Development Indicators, specifically economy-and-growth.csv (GDP) and social-development.csv (life expectancy).
  • Indicators used: NY.GDP.PCAP.KD (GDP per capita, constant 2010 US$). For life expectancy, the cleaned source files do not include the World Bank’s combined total indicator SP.DYN.LE00.IN, so we computed it as the unweighted mean of SP.DYN.LE00.MA.IN (male) and SP.DYN.LE00.FE.IN (female). The result differs from the official total by roughly 0.1 years and does not change any conclusion.
  • Time slice: three of the four charts use the 2019 cross section (the most recent year with broad coverage in the cleaned files). The longitudinal FOR chart 2 extends to 1960 to 2019 for six countries.
  • Country universe: 179 entities for which both indicators are non null in 2019. Aggregate rows ("World", "OECD members", regional groupings) were excluded. Same filter applied identically across all four charts.
  • Joins and nulls: source files contain zero duplicate (Country Name, Year) rows. Inner join on those keys, then drop nulls.
  • Validation pass: using the data:validate-data skill. Zero duplicate keys; all anchor country values referenced in the report were spot checked against published World Bank values; R² recomputed at 0.70.
  • Fit: OLS of life expectancy on log10(GDP). Slope = +9.9 years per 10x increase in GDP, R² = 0.70. The shaded band on FOR chart 1 is mean fit ± 1.96 residual standard deviations; this is a residual spread, not a formal confidence interval on the regression mean. The chart legend and reading guide describe it that way.
  • No jitter: every scatter point sits at its true 2019 value. We considered jittering low GDP countries on AGAINST chart 1 to declutter the left wall and rejected it as undisclosed deception. The crammed left side is the chart’s argument.
  • Color blindness mitigation: red and green carry argumentative weight on AGAINST chart 1 and AGAINST chart 2. We use shape redundancy (red circles vs. green squares) and explicit text labels so the encoding is readable without relying on color alone.
  • Reproducibility: generate_charts.py at the repo root, with the SWD style helpers under helpers/, regenerates every chart on this page from the source CSVs.

This HTML embeds all four chart images inline as base64, so the page is self contained and renders in any viewer without depending on separate image files. The source repository also ships standalone PNGs under images/ alongside the chart generation scripts, in case future readers want to edit the charts without re rendering the whole page.

Files in this submission: index.html, images/pro_viz.png, images/pro_viz2.png, images/con_viz.png, images/con_viz2.png, generate_charts.py, helpers/, and PROJECT2_AGENT_CONTEXT.md.
